clue.text: Nightspot strike

definitions.meaning: the place with a late licence, a dance floor and a queue outside — the noun sense
to hit something hard with a heavy stick, which is the verb sense of the same four letters

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, nothing to shuffle and no indicator anywhere: a noun and a verb are simply set side by side, and the clue never says which of them is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Nightspot is the noun, a venue for dancing; strike is the verb, to beat with a heavy stick, and one short word covers both senses.

clue.text: Vice-consul unwisely decisive

indicators.note: Doing a thing unwisely is doing it without care, and letters handled carelessly do not come out in the order they went in.

parts.note: ten letters go in and ten come out, with the hyphen counting for nothing

explanation.walkthrough: A vice-consul is a junior diplomat, and a job title dropped into a clue with no work to do on the surface is nearly always ten letters waiting to be shaken.
explanation.definitionFit: decisive: evidence that settles a question for good, so the adjective describes proof that ends the argument rather than a person who chooses quickly.

clue.text: Merrily reunited, embracing queen that's snubbed

indicators.note: Merry is the polite word for tipsy, and a tipsy word cannot keep its letters standing in the right places.
To embrace is to fold your arms right round something, so the piece named next ends up inside the others rather than beside them.

parts.note: the eight letters re-ordered first, then opened up in the middle
Qu. is the dictionary's short form for queen, the pair of letters rather than the single Q of chess

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a cheerful family reunion with royalty present, and every word of it is machinery. Qu. for queen is the abbreviation a dictionary keeps and a solver forgets.
explanation.definitionFit: snubbed: feelings offered and never returned leave the one who offered them rebuffed, which is the past-participle sense the definition supplies.

clue.text: Affected to welcome company that's smart, irritatingly so

indicators.note: To welcome someone is to take them indoors, so the short piece is admitted into the middle of the longer one.

parts.note: a precious manner is an affected one — mannered, too refined by half
CO is the tag that follows a firm's name, as in Smith & Co

explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers a smug host greeting a business partner. 'Affected' is not the feelings sense but the mannered one, and it is the word that has to open up.
explanation.definitionFit: smart, irritatingly so: a child clever beyond their years, with the second half of the definition supplying the grating quality the plain word lacks.

clue.text: Disturbed, with hair on end, ran away

indicators.note: Hair standing on end points straight upwards, and in a down entry a word read upwards arrives back to front.

parts.note: fur is the hair an animal wears, and it climbs the grid before it joins anything
the past tense of flee is what somebody who ran away did

explanation.walkthrough: 'Disturbed' sits at the head of the clue looking exactly like an anagram signal, and nothing beside it is shuffled: it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Disturbed: put out of calm, whether the surface of a pond or a person's composure, so the participle covers both feathers and feelings.

clue.text: Having entered church, tends to purify

indicators.note: Something that has entered a building is now within it, so one piece finishes up in the middle of the other.

parts.note: CE is the Church of England, the standard shortening on any British form
a mast that tends to starboard leans that way — the inclining sense, not the caring one

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has a devout gardener at work, and the trap is 'tends': not looking after anything, but sloping.
explanation.definitionFit: purify: to make clean again by washing away what soils it, the same verb whether the dirt is on a wound or on a conscience.

clue.text: King, seeing that, to pass waterway in fold

parts.note: CR is Charles Rex, the cipher of the current British king, the way ER stood for the late Queen
as can mean since — 'as it's raining, we'll stay in'
pass me the salt and hand me the salt are the same request
a burn is a stream in Scotland and the north of England, as in Bannockburn

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a monarch fording a river on his way somewhere. The definition is the last word, in the sense a poker player or a failing business uses it.
explanation.definitionFit: fold: a business that folds collapses and stops trading, and the answer is the vivid phrase for failing that spectacularly.

clue.text: Cockney tramp that's found among the reeds

parts.note: a hobo is a wanderer who rides the freight trains, the American word for a tramp

indicators.note: A Cockney accent drops the aitch off the front of a word, so what is left begins on the vowel — and the clue leaves you to notice that the rest is a matter of sound.

parts.note: with the aitch gone, the two syllables that remain are said exactly the way the four-letter spelling is

explanation.walkthrough: 'Reeds' pulls you to a riverbank, and the reeds meant are the strips of cane a woodwind player blows between. Everything else in the clue is pronunciation.
explanation.definitionFit: found among the reeds: an orchestra's reed section is the woodwind, and this double-reed instrument sits in it — the definition names the family, not the object.

clue.text: Posed first of stiff challenges for schoolchildren

parts.note: somebody who sat for a portrait posed for it

indicators.note: The phrase picks the letter a word begins on rather than the word itself, so only one character of what follows is wanted.

parts.note: the letter that word opens on

explanation.walkthrough: 'Posed' reads as the verb for asking a question, which is how challenges get into the surface. The sense wanted is what a portrait sitter does.
explanation.definitionFit: challenges for schoolchildren: the national curriculum tests English pupils sit at seven and eleven, named by what they put in front of a child.

clue.text: How to describe 'nudism' in the extreme? It's accepted behaviour

indicators.note: The phrase means as far as a thing goes, so it points at the two far ends of the quoted word and nothing between them.

parts.note: the opening letter of the quoted word
with two candidates and no way to choose, the honest description names one alternative or the other, and the joining word gets written down too
the letter the same quoted word finishes on

explanation.walkthrough: The word in quotation marks is not there to be defined, only measured. Name its two ends and the little word that joins any pair of alternatives sits between them.
explanation.definitionFit: accepted behaviour: the standard a group takes for granted, so the noun is what people do by default rather than any written rule.

clue.text: Like some laundry ready to put away? Ish

definitions.text: Like some laundry ready to put away?
definitions.meaning: washing only reaches the drawer once somebody has divided it into piles, and this is the state it is in then
the suffix people tack onto a word to mean roughly, or up to a point

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the joke: one reading needs the everyday noun for a sorting, the other is the idiom for approximately, and the three words are identical.
explanation.definitionFit: Both halves are the same phrase read twice: laundry that has been through a sorting, and the idiom meaning to a limited extent, which is what 'ish' does.

clue.text: Vandal all but leering unpleasantly: let's move on

indicators.note: All but something means everything except a little of it, and what is left out here is the final letter of the word that follows.
Behaving unpleasantly is behaving badly, and letters treated badly refuse to stay in the order they were printed.

parts.note: six letters straight off the page, thrown into the mix untouched
six more, the whole of that word except the G at the end

explanation.walkthrough: 'Vandal' and 'leering' build a nasty little scene and neither means anything: they are twelve letters. The colon is where the sentence turns into what people say after a mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: let's move on: what you say to shrug off a mistake and count the loss as experience, an idiom belonging to the phrase as a whole.

clue.text: £51: midday meal that includes booze

parts.note: Roman numerals: fifty is L and one is I
a quid is a pound in British slang, so the sign is read as the word you would say
the meal eaten in the middle of the day

explanation.walkthrough: £51 is written sign first and said number first — fifty-one quid — so the wordplay follows the ear. 'Midday meal' then earns its keep twice, once as letters and once inside the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: midday meal that includes booze: the wry name for a lunch where the drink replaces the food, so the definition describes the custom rather than translating a word.

clue.text: Bisque's prepared with coconut, regularly aiming to please

indicators.note: Preparing an ingredient means chopping and mixing it before use, which is licence to ignore the order the letters arrive in.
Taken at regular intervals means every second one, so two of the seven letters beside it are picked up and the rest passed over.

parts.note: a bisque is a smooth shellfish soup, and the apostrophe-s hands over a seventh letter
the second, fourth and sixth letters of the word, read in order

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a recipe. The apostrophe-s is the giveaway: it is not a verb here at all, just one more letter for the mixture.
explanation.definitionFit: aiming to please: fawning attentiveness, the servility of someone who agrees with everything — not the plain helpfulness the words sound like.

clue.text: A setter had to dance: it's not a good look

indicators.note: Dancers keep changing places on the floor, and letters told to dance swap positions the same way.

parts.note: ten letters go in and every one of them is used once

explanation.walkthrough: 'A setter' normally means the compiler himself, or a breed of dog. Here it is neither, just three short words holding ten letters.
explanation.definitionFit: not a good look: the withering glare one person turns on another, so 'look' is the noun for an expression and the litotes supplies its hostility.

clue.text: A little bookie's tip endangered a little bit of money

indicators.note: A little of something is a portion rather than the whole, so a short run taken out of the words as printed is what is wanted.

parts.note: the run begins on the last letter of the first word and stops four letters into the last, crossing both gaps

explanation.walkthrough: 'Endangered' is a long word doing very little on the surface, and a setter reaching for one that ungainly is usually building a hiding place.
explanation.definitionFit: a little bit of money: a fixed modest payment made at regular intervals to a curate or a student, so the smallness is part of the meaning.

clue.text: Dignify the Spanish worthy across the Pyrénées heading west

indicators.note: The mountains are the border between Spain and France, so a word carried over them is wanted in the other country's language.
In an across entry west is leftwards, so the letters are read from the far end back towards the start.

parts.note: el is the masculine definite article in Spanish
the feminine of bon — a worthy cause is 'une bonne cause' in French

explanation.walkthrough: Two languages in one clue: the article is Spanish, the adjective French, and the mountain range in the middle is what tells you the second one has changed country.
explanation.definitionFit: Dignify: to raise somebody in rank, which is what a peerage does — the verb sense of conferring standing rather than merely honouring.

clue.text: Drive around volcano somewhere in Indochina

indicators.note: Put one thing around another and it wraps it, so the short word opens up and the rest lands in the gap.

parts.note: vim is energy or push — 'vim and vigour' — the noun, not the verb for steering
Etna is the Sicilian volcano, four convenient letters every setter keeps handy

explanation.walkthrough: The surface has somebody motoring past a mountain. 'Drive' is the trap: not the journey but the get-up-and-go.
explanation.definitionFit: somewhere in Indochina: Indochina is the peninsula east of India, and the country is one of the three that make it up, so this is definition by region.

clue.text: Emotionally affect topless hooligan in retreat

indicators.note: Topless is without the top, and the top of a word written down a grid is the letter it starts on.

parts.note: a film that moves you has worked on your feelings
a lout is a loud, aggressive young man, and he arrives here without his first letter

explanation.walkthrough: A definition-shaped phrase opens the clue, which is where a definition usually sits — and here those two words are the wordplay, with the definition left alone at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: retreat: to withdraw from a position, the verb an army obeys when ordered off ground it holds, rather than a place of quiet.

clue.text: Reformed inmate welcoming drop of bonhomie — it's all around

indicators.note: Reformed means made again in a new shape, and letters re-made that way abandon the arrangement the clue printed.
A host welcoming a guest takes them into the house, so this single letter goes inside rather than alongside.

parts.note: six letters shaken into a new order and then opened up

indicators.note: A drop is the least you can take of anything poured, and the least of a written word is the letter it opens on.

parts.note: bonhomie is French for hearty good humour, and only its opening letter is taken

explanation.walkthrough: 'Reformed inmate' tells a whole story in two words, and both of them are machinery — the story is the disguise, and the dash hides the join to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: all around: describing sound or light that surrounds you instead of coming from one point, the adjective a room's background music is given.

clue.text: Lack awareness of stomach muscles, did you say?

parts.note: abs is the gym shorthand for the abdominal muscles

indicators.note: The question asks how the phrase sounds rather than how it is written, so the spelling has to follow the ear.

parts.note: a sense of something is an awareness of it, and run straight on from the piece before it the S is heard only once

explanation.walkthrough: Say the two pieces one after another and the join vanishes: a single S does the work of two, which is why the spelling that comes out looks nothing like the parts.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack: the noun for a thing simply not being there — 'in the lack of evidence' is 'in the absence of evidence' — rather than the verb to want something.

clue.text: England cricket captain no more after charge announced, he wrote

definitions.note: The definition points at a person by what he did rather than offering a synonym: 'he wrote' is crossword shorthand for an author, and the answer is a surname.

indicators.note: Announcing something is saying it out loud, so what is wanted is the sound of the word rather than its spelling.
After puts one piece behind the other, so the sounded word comes first and the name follows it.

parts.note: a levy is a charge imposed by an authority, and said aloud it gives no hint of which spelling is meant
Andrew Strauss captained England at cricket and retired years ago, which is what 'no more' marks

explanation.walkthrough: Two other men crowd in: the cricketer whose name is borrowed whole, and the maker of jeans the surname brings to mind. The one wanted is neither.
explanation.definitionFit: he wrote: Claude Lévi-Strauss, the French anthropologist of myth and kinship, is named by his books the way setters name any author.

clue.text: Leaving France, get to make lasting impression

indicators.note: Leaving a country means going out of it, so the letter standing for that country departs from the word.

parts.note: to fetch something is to go and get it
F is the international code for France, the letter on the back of French cars

explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaving France' opens the clue like the start of a travel story and is pure instruction; the impression meant is bitten into metal, not made on a person.
explanation.definitionFit: make lasting impression: to cut a line into metal or glass with acid, so the mark is permanent — the figurative 'etched in memory' comes from that.

clue.text: Primarily punctilious, reserved in manner?

parts.note: primarily means in the first place, so each of the four words that follow hands over the letter it begins with, in the order printed

explanation.walkthrough: An &lit: read once, the whole sentence — first word included — describes a fussily correct sort of person; read again, four of its words give up their opening letters and nothing is left over.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight as a description of stiff, punctilious correctness, so definition and wordplay are the very same words.

clue.text: Unexpected event: performer getting drinks for everyone

parts.note: in music hall each act on the bill was a turn, and the word covers the performer as well as the performance
in a British pub one person buys a round, a drink for every member of the group at once

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a night out, and the colon is the only thing dividing the definition from the wordplay — the first two words are all the definition there is.
explanation.definitionFit: Unexpected event: a sudden reversal of fortune or policy, so the noun names the change itself rather than the thing that changed.

clue.text: On reflection, Bard's river is one full of light

indicators.note: A reflection shows a thing the wrong way round, so the letters are read from the far end back.

parts.note: the river at Stratford, which is why Shakespeare is the Bard of Avon

explanation.walkthrough: 'On reflection' opens the clue as though the setter were having second thoughts, and it is the instruction. The water in the surface is what makes the reflection plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: one full of light: a star that suddenly flares far brighter than before, so 'one' stands for a star and the light is the outburst.

clue.text: Geography / history unit: shame I failed?

indicators.note: Something that has failed has fallen apart, and letters in that state no longer hold the shape they were given.

parts.note: ten letters in all, counting the single letter I as one of them

explanation.walkthrough: The slash is not punctuation to skip past: it separates two example subjects from the wordplay, and 'unit' joins the mixture rather than describing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Geography / history: two of the school subjects grouped under this heading, so the definition works by example rather than by synonym.

clue.text: Everyman — scenes — regularly falling out — that's understood

parts.note: the setter signs the puzzle with that name, and a setter writing about himself uses the first-person pronoun

indicators.note: Letters dropping away at regular intervals leave every other one standing, so the word is read taking one and skipping one.

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters, once the other three have dropped away

explanation.walkthrough: The setter's own name in a clue is nearly always the pronoun rather than a person, and the dashes make three separate fragments look like one aside.
explanation.definitionFit: that's understood: the two words you say to show a thing has just been grasped, an idiom for the whole phrase rather than for either word in it.
